lessons.subject: ELA
lessons.title: Goodall: craft, contrast and perspective
teach: The author’s purpose is the reason the author wrote the text. Ask: What does Goodall want readers to learn or understand?
Goodall informs readers about her research and what she learned about chimps. She tells about her own experiences and explains why the discoveries mattered.
Her feelings make the memoir interesting, but entertainment is not her only purpose. Her observations also teach readers about chimpanzees.
A personality trait describes how a person usually thinks or acts. Choose a trait, name an action from the text, and explain how the action shows that trait.
Goodall is persistent: she keeps trying after setbacks. She is patient: she gives the chimps time to get used to her. She is careful: she writes down details from her observations.
Her success came from these choices and from help from other people. Success does not mean she was never afraid or that she did everything alone.
A memoir is nonfiction about real experiences from the writer’s own life. The writer looks back and explains what those experiences meant.
Goodall took part in the events she describes. She uses first-person words such as I and my, tells what happened, and shares her thoughts and feelings.
The word I alone does not prove that a text is a memoir. A made-up story can use I, too. A memoir tells real personal experiences and reflects on them.
A memoir usually focuses on a meaningful part of a person’s life. An autobiography usually covers more of the person’s life.

model.prompt: Original parallel: “I tried Monday. No sound. Tuesday, no sound. Wednesday—one clear note!” How do craft choices work?
model.reasoning: Repeated failed attempts establish a pattern. The dash marks a turn away from that pattern. The exclamation emphasizes the narrator’s excitement. Link effect to idea: progress matters more because effort and delay were shown.
model.answer: The repetition emphasizes repeated failure; the dash marks the turning point and the exclamation conveys excitement. Together they make the eventual success feel earned.

lessons.subject: ELA
lessons.title: Goodall: evidence changes an explanation
teach: Goodall learned that chimps use tools and can change materials to make tools. David stripped leaves from a twig before using it to get termites.
She learned that chimps are individuals. They have different personalities, and their family relationships affect how they act.
She also saw young chimps learning from others. Chimps use calls and gestures to share information. Some gestures look like human gestures, but their calls are not the same as human language.
When you explain a discovery, tell what she saw and what it helped her understand. Do not make a bigger claim than the detail supports.

model.prompt: An original parallel case: An observer sees a crow bend wire and use it to lift a food basket. What claim can she support?
model.reasoning: Separate observed behavior: the crow changed wire and used it. Make a limited claim: this crow modified an object for a task. Reject the overclaim: one observation does not prove every crow does this. Ask what would strengthen the claim: repeated observations, more individuals and conditions.
model.answer: The observation supports that this crow modified an object to obtain food. It does not establish that every crow does so; repeated varied observations would test the broader claim.

lessons.subject: ELA
lessons.title: START HERE · Goodall study guide · Grade 6
teach: A memoir tells about real events in the writer’s life. Read Goodall’s whole memoir first so you understand what happened.
On your second reading, ask: What problems did she face? What did she learn? How did her work change over time?
When a question names a paragraph, reread that paragraph and the sentences around it. Use a detail from that part to explain your answer.
The topic is what a text is about. This memoir is about Jane Goodall’s work with chimpanzees. The main idea tells the most important point about that topic.
Goodall keeps trying, watches carefully, gains the chimps’ trust, and makes discoveries. Help from other people also supports her work.
A good main idea fits the whole memoir. Check it against the beginning, middle, and ending. One exciting event is a detail, not the main idea of the whole text.
Read the sentence around an unfamiliar word. Try a meaning, put it into the sentence, and check whether it makes sense.
Vanished means disappeared. “The deer vanished into the bushes” means the deer could no longer be seen.
Miserable means very unhappy or uncomfortable. “The cold rain made the wait miserable” shows discomfort.
Irritable means easily annoyed. An irritable person may get upset over a small interruption.
Threateningly means in a way that warns of possible harm. A dog that growls threateningly may be warning someone to stay back.
Impetuous means acting quickly without thinking enough. Cutting fabric before measuring it can be an impetuous choice.
Dominate means to control or have power over. Someone who interrupts everyone may try to dominate a discussion.

A subject tells who or what a clause is about. A verb tells an action or a state of being. A clause has a subject and a verb. An independent clause is a complete thought: “Maya kept notes.” A dependent clause needs more to finish its meaning: “Although the camera failed.”
Use a comma before and, but, or so when the word joins two complete thoughts: “The camera failed, but Maya kept notes.” Each side can stand alone.
Do not add a comma just because you see and. “Maya checked the camera and changed the battery” has one subject doing two actions.
Use a comma after a dependent clause at the beginning: “Although the camera failed, Maya kept notes.” The comma goes where the opening clause ends.
Use a comma after a long opening phrase: “After several hours beside the marsh, Maya packed her notebook.” This opening is a phrase because it does not have its own subject and verb.
Use a comma after an opening transition: “For example, Maya recorded the time.” Other examples are “In fact,” and “After all,”.
Use commas in a list of three or more things: “She packed paper, pencils, and binoculars.” In these questions, include the comma before the final and. This is called a serial comma.
The author’s purpose is the reason the author wrote the text. Ask: What does Goodall want readers to learn or understand?
Goodall informs readers about her research and what she learned about chimps. She tells about her own experiences and explains why the discoveries mattered.
Her feelings make the memoir interesting, but entertainment is not her only purpose. Her observations also teach readers about chimpanzees.
Goodall learned that chimps use tools and can change materials to make tools. David stripped leaves from a twig before using it to get termites.
She learned that chimps are individuals. They have different personalities, and their family relationships affect how they act.
She also saw young chimps learning from others. Chimps use calls and gestures to share information. Some gestures look like human gestures, but their calls are not the same as human language.
When you explain a discovery, tell what she saw and what it helped her understand. Do not make a bigger claim than the detail supports.
A personality trait describes how a person usually thinks or acts. Choose a trait, name an action from the text, and explain how the action shows that trait.
Goodall is persistent: she keeps trying after setbacks. She is patient: she gives the chimps time to get used to her. She is careful: she writes down details from her observations.
Her success came from these choices and from help from other people. Success does not mean she was never afraid or that she did everything alone.
A memoir is nonfiction about real experiences from the writer’s own life. The writer looks back and explains what those experiences meant.
Goodall took part in the events she describes. She uses first-person words such as I and my, tells what happened, and shares her thoughts and feelings.
The word I alone does not prove that a text is a memoir. A made-up story can use I, too. A memoir tells real personal experiences and reflects on them.
A memoir usually focuses on a meaningful part of a person’s life. An autobiography usually covers more of the person’s life.

model.prompt: Original parallel scenario: In a real first-person account, Noor recalls months of failed garden measurements, explains how she changed her method and reflects on learning to trust checked evidence. Explain purpose, a trait and memoir features.
model.reasoning: Separate purpose from topic: she explains a learning process and its meaning, not simply “gardens.” Connect action to trait: repeated checking and revised measurements support careful persistence. Establish genre using real personal events, selected months and reflection; “I” alone would not prove memoir.
model.answer: Noor informs readers about developing reliable measurements and reflects on learning. Revising and checking evidence supports careful persistence. The real first-person experiences from a selected period, together with reflection, make this a memoir.

lessons.subject: MATH
lessons.title: Big8: retrieve, derive and use exact forms
teach: The teacher’s eight families are1/2,1/3,1/4,1/5,1/8,1/9,1/10 and2/3. Retrieve all three forms, then use a benchmark to derive a new value.

Exact families:1/2=.5=50%;1/3=.333…=33⅓%;1/4=.25=25%;1/5=.2=20%;1/8=.125=12.5%;1/9=.111…=11⅑%;1/10=.1=10%;2/3=.666…=66⅔%. The ellipsis means the digit continues; a rounded decimal is not exactly equal.
A percent is a rate per hundred. Use decimal×100 to express a decimal as percent, and percent÷100 for the reverse. Check whether the size makes sense.
Recognition is not the same as recall. For spelling or number facts, hide the target before retrieving it. Then explain or apply the value in a new problem.

model.prompt: Original application: a pattern needs5/8 of a meter of fabric. Express that as a decimal and percent of one meter.
model.reasoning: Use1/8=.125. Multiply5×.125=.625 meter. Convert.625×100=62.5%. Check:5/8 is greater than1/2 and less than3/4, so62.5% fits.
model.answer: 5/8=.625=62.5% of one meter. It is between1/2 and3/4, so the converted value is reasonable.

lessons.subject: MATH
lessons.title: Expressions: describe a relationship before calculating
teach: A variable represents a number or quantity. A constant is fixed in the situation. An expression represents a quantity; an equation states that two expressions are equal.
A coefficient is a number multiplying a variable. In 4n, 4 is the coefficient; it means four groups of n. In n + 4, the 4 is added, so it is a constant term rather than the coefficient of n.

Read the situation before translating. In an original art-supply model, a fixed delivery fee plus a cost for each sketchbook needs both parts. The unit explains the operation: dollars per sketchbook multiplied by number of sketchbooks gives dollars.
To evaluate, replace the variable with its stated value, keep parentheses and follow the order of operations. Multiplication written beside a variable is still multiplication.

model.prompt: Original situation: sketchbooks cost $4 each plus a $3 delivery fee. Express and evaluate the cost for 5 sketchbooks.
model.reasoning: Define n as the number of sketchbooks. Variable cost is4n; the fixed fee is3. Expression:4n+3. At n=5:4×5+3=23 dollars. Check reasonableness:5 books alone cost20 dollars; delivery adds 3.
model.answer: With n sketchbooks, cost is4n+3 dollars. At n=5 the cost is23 dollars;20 for books plus3 delivery. The units and fixed/repeated costs support the model.

lessons.subject: MATH
lessons.title: Expressions: powers, grouping and substitution
teach: An exponent counts repeated equal factors, not multiplication by the exponent:3²=3×3=9, while3×2=6. The base is the factor being repeated.

Evaluate grouping first, then powers, then multiplication/division left to right, then addition/subtraction left to right. Multiplication does not always go before division; addition does not always go before subtraction.
When substituting, replace EVERY occurrence of each variable. Write multiplication explicitly before calculating:2ab means2×a×b, not a three-digit number.

Scope matters: (ab)² squares the whole product; a+b² squares only b. Parentheses show exactly what an exponent or operation applies to. The current Pumpkin activity requires multi-variable substitution and powers, beyond single-variable addition.

model.prompt: Original expression:2+(ab)² when a=2 and b=3. Compare it with 2+ab².
model.reasoning: Substitute:2+(2×3)². Compute grouped product6, then square36, then add2. For2+ab², square3 first, then multiply2×9 and add2.
model.answer: 2+(ab)²=38, while2+ab²=20 at these values. The exponent’s scope changes the result.

lessons.subject: MATH
lessons.title: Rational numbers: order, absolute value and coordinate distance
teach: Compare values on a common scale. For negative numbers, farther left is smaller. Convert a fraction to an exact decimal when possible, or compare fractions with a reliable common representation.
Absolute value is distance from zero, so it is nonnegative. The number with greatest absolute value need not be the greatest signed number.

For horizontal points with the same y, use the absolute difference of x-coordinates. For vertical points with the same x, use the absolute difference of y-coordinates. Include units and use the graph scale when working from a diagram.
The assigned two-page Week12 sheet contains rational-number least-to-greatest sets and horizontal/vertical distances with fractions and decimals. Do not count grid endpoints or swap x and y.

model.prompt: Original points A=(−1.5,2) and B=(2.25,2). Find the distance and explain why it is positive.
model.reasoning: Both y-coordinates equal2, so movement is horizontal. Subtract x-values:2.25−(−1.5)=3.75. Distance is the nonnegative separation; reversing subtraction and taking absolute value gives the same result.
model.answer: The horizontal distance is3.75 units. It is separation, not a signed direction.

lessons.subject: MATH
lessons.title: Problem-solving spiral: choose the method and prove it
teach: Multi-step decimal problems: first compute total needed, then subtract what is already available. Distinguish “how much total” from “how much more.” Show cups or meters throughout.
Decimal division: scale dividend and divisor by the same power of10 so the quotient is unchanged. Check by multiplication and estimate whether the quotient’s size is reasonable.
Unit rates: divide the requested numerator quantity by the denominator quantity. Miles per gallon means miles÷gallons; minutes per mile means minutes÷miles. Reversing units produces a different rate.
Division by a fraction asks how many groups of that size fit. Rename mixed numbers as improper fractions; multiplying by the reciprocal gives the quotient. Verify quotient×divisor=dividend.

Percent of a whole: part÷whole gives the decimal rate, then multiply by100 for percent. State the reference whole before computing. A result above100% can be valid only when the part exceeds the chosen whole.
Whole-number division: preserve place value, including a zero in the quotient when needed. Verify by multiplication rather than choosing a digit pattern.
Decimal subtraction: line up decimal points and like place values, adding trailing zeros if useful. “Subtracta fromb” meansb−a.
Ratios: retain the requested order and distinguish part:part from part:whole. Simplify both terms by the same nonzero factor. Equivalent ratios preserve the relationship.

model.prompt: Original design task: a pattern needs1.5 meters per item for 4 items. You own2.25 meters. A store sells fabric at$6 per meter. How much extra fabric and what cost are needed?
model.reasoning: Total fabric:1.5×4=6 meters. Extra needed:6−2.25=3.75 meters. Additional cost:3.75×6=22.50 dollars. Check that buying3.75 meters brings the total to6, enough for all4 items.
model.answer: Buy3.75 meters for$22.50 under the stated constant price, before any additional fees. The total-needed and additional-needed quantities are different.

lessons.subject: SCI
lessons.title: Ecology vocabulary: effects on both partners
teach: Symbiosis is the relationship noun; symbiotic is the describing adjective. These refer to close cross-species associations. They do not guarantee both partners benefit. Read the effects on each participant before choosing a more specific classification.

Use an effects table: mutualism is benefit/benefit, parasitism is benefit/harm, commensalism is benefit/no known effect. Host identifies the provider of habitat/resources; it does not by itself establish harm. Explain what evidence would change your conclusion.
Study every term card in this group: say the meaning, explain the example, reject the nonexample, and apply the scientific boundary. Then close the cards for the checks.

model.prompt: Original association model: gut organisms receive food and shelter while supplying useful vitamins to an animal. Name the host, explain the benefit to each, and distinguish the relationship noun from its adjective.
model.reasoning: Identify exactly which organisms, environment or relationship is being described. Choose a term whose meaning fits those details. Compare the closest alternative and explain why it does not fit. Keep the conclusion limited to the given evidence and conditions.
model.answer: The animal is the host because it supplies habitat/resources. The described vitamin-producing partners and animal each benefit, so this case is mutualism. The relationship noun is symbiosis and the adjective is symbiotic. Harm to the host would instead support parasitism; benefit with no partner effect would support commensalism.

lessons.subject: SCI
lessons.title: Ecology vocabulary: feeding roles and diets
teach: Separate broad role, diet and pathway level. A consumer can be a herbivore, carnivore or omnivore. Predator/prey identifies the participants in a particular feeding interaction. Tertiary consumer identifies a position on one stated path.

Start from a producer and follow arrows. Primary eats a producer; secondary eats primary; tertiary eats secondary. A tertiary consumer need not be the highest organism in a longer path. An omnivore can occupy more than one level, so always name the path.
Study every term card in this group: say the meaning, explain the example, reject the nonexample, and apply the scientific boundary. Then close the cards for the checks.

model.prompt: Original feeding model: grass→grasshopper→frog→snake. Grass is producer; the other organisms are consumers. The frog is predator relative to the grasshopper and prey relative to the snake; the snake is tertiary on this path.
model.reasoning: Identify exactly which organisms, environment or relationship is being described. Choose a term whose meaning fits those details. Compare the closest alternative and explain why it does not fit. Keep the conclusion limited to the given evidence and conditions.
model.answer: Grass is the producer; grasshopper, frog and snake are consumers. The grasshopper is primary, frog secondary and snake tertiary in this chain. The frog is predator of the grasshopper and prey of the snake. Diet categories require the actual foods stated; an omnivore can occupy different levels on different paths.

lessons.subject: SCI
lessons.title: Ecology vocabulary: from one organism to the biosphere
teach: Use nesting and contrast to make the words meaningful: one organism, a same-species population, interacting populations as a community, and organisms plus abiotic conditions as an ecosystem. The biosphere is the global life scope. A biome groups broad climate-and-community regions; it is not simply one step in the local nested list.

For every example, say what is included and what is left out. A community includes living populations; an ecosystem also considers nonliving conditions. Biotic and abiotic are describing words, not two new organization levels.
Study every term card in this group: say the meaning, explain the example, reject the nonexample, and apply the scientific boundary. Then close the cards for the checks.

model.prompt: Original park model: one oak → all oaks of that species in the park → interacting living populations → those populations with water, light and soil conditions. Explain what changes at each step.
model.reasoning: Identify exactly which organisms, environment or relationship is being described. Choose a term whose meaning fits those details. Compare the closest alternative and explain why it does not fit. Keep the conclusion limited to the given evidence and conditions.
model.answer: The single oak is an organism; all local oaks of that species are a population; the interacting living populations form a community; adding water, light and soil conditions gives an ecosystem. The biome is a broad climate/community region, and the biosphere is Earth’s global life scope. Biotic/abiotic describe factors rather than add nesting levels.

lessons.subject: SCI
lessons.title: Ecology vocabulary: models and processing remains
teach: A chain traces one energy route; a web combines routes; an energy pyramid compares available energy by level. These models answer different questions and omit details. Do not read a pyramid as a map or assume it shows the exact number of individuals.

A scavenger consumes dead remains. Decomposers such as fungi and bacteria break down remains and waste. Both help process material, but they are not identical mechanisms. Matter is returned and reused; usable energy transfers and disperses rather than cycling back identically.
Study every term card in this group: say the meaning, explain the example, reject the nonexample, and apply the scientific boundary. Then close the cards for the checks.

model.prompt: Original pond model: algae feeds snails and insect larvae, both eaten by fish. Trace one chain, then the whole web. Compare usable energy by level, and add decomposers acting on material from every level.
model.reasoning: Identify exactly which organisms, environment or relationship is being described. Choose a term whose meaning fits those details. Compare the closest alternative and explain why it does not fit. Keep the conclusion limited to the given evidence and conditions.
model.answer: Algae→snail→fish is one food chain; adding algae→insect larva→fish makes connected paths in a food web. An energy pyramid represents less usable energy reaching higher levels. Decomposers break down remains/wastes from all levels; scavengers consume dead remains. Nutrients can return to the environment while energy transfers and disperses.

lessons.subject: SCI
lessons.title: Ecology vocabulary: resource use, limits and introductions
teach: A species can share a habitat yet use different resources. Explain a niche with what, when and how resources are used. Then identify the condition that currently limits a population and how that affects supportable population size.

Native and invasive describe different things: natural regional occurrence versus a harmful nonnative introduction. Not all introduced organisms are invasive. An adaptation is an inherited trait related to conditions, not a decision an individual makes because it needs to change.
Study every term card in this group: say the meaning, explain the example, reject the nonexample, and apply the scientific boundary. Then close the cards for the checks.

model.prompt: Original garden model: a plant introduced by people spreads and shades out native seedlings. The lost light limits seedling growth. Identify origin, harm, resource mechanism and the evidence needed to estimate longer-term population support.
model.reasoning: Identify exactly which organisms, environment or relationship is being described. Choose a term whose meaning fits those details. Compare the closest alternative and explain why it does not fit. Keep the conclusion limited to the given evidence and conditions.
model.answer: The plant is nonnative, and its documented harmful spread supports invasive status. Reduced light is a limiting factor for seedlings. Its niche includes its resource use and interactions; estimating carrying capacity needs more resource and population evidence. No individual acquires an inherited adaptation simply because it needs one.

lessons.subject: SCI
lessons.title: Ecology: resources, competition and changing limits
teach: A habitat is where an organism lives. A niche includes how it uses resources and interacts. Two species sharing a place do not automatically compete for every resource.

Competition happens when organisms need the same limited resource. Within one species it is intraspecific; between species it is interspecific. Ask which resource, which organisms and what evidence shows limitation.

Population density concerns individuals per area or volume. Carrying capacity concerns how many of a particular population the environment can support under current conditions. The capacity can change when water, food, shelter or other conditions change.

The uploaded notes pair giraffes and zebras as browsers. Scientific correction: zebras primarily graze grasses; giraffes browse woody leaves. Use their different feeding as a way to examine reduced overlap, not as proof of identical niches. A simplified population diagram is a model, not a guarantee of a fixed cycle.

model.prompt: Original scenario: two groups of birds live in one park. One eats ground seeds; the other catches insects above the pond. A dry season reduces the pond insects.
model.reasoning: Identify the resource affected: pond insects. Name the group most directly affected: insect-feeding birds. Do not assume seed-eating birds face identical effects. Predict with a condition: if alternate food is limited, survival/reproduction may decrease. Name evidence needed: food availability, diet and population records.
model.answer: The insect-feeding birds lose a food resource. They may decline if alternatives are insufficient; diet, food and population evidence is needed before predicting the exact change.

lessons.subject: SCI
lessons.title: Relationships: classify from evidence, not animal names
teach: Classify an interaction by what happens to the organisms. Competition involves a shared limited resource. Predation involves consuming prey. Symbiosis is a close relationship between different species.

Mutualism benefits both participants. Parasitism benefits the parasite and harms the host. Commensalism benefits one without a known effect on the other. A species’ name alone cannot reveal the relationship; inspect the described evidence.
A host provides resources or a place to live. Not every host relationship is parasitism: ask whether harm is described. Benefits and harms can also depend on the context.
The two organisms matter, but so do the conditions. Use “in this described interaction” to keep a classification tied to evidence. Avoid assigning moral labels such as good or bad animals.

model.prompt: Original cases: a tick feeds on a deer; two deer compete for scarce plants; a deer eats a plant; bacteria receive food in an animal’s gut and supply useful vitamins.
model.reasoning: Tick/deer: parasite obtains food while host is harmed. Deer/deer: same-species competition for limited plants. Deer/plant: herbivory, a feeding interaction. Gut bacteria/animal in the described case: each receives a benefit. State the evidence that would change a classification.
model.answer: The tick/deer case is parasitism; deer competing for scarce plants is competition; gut partners with benefits to both is mutualism. Each classification needs effects or resource evidence.

lessons.subject: SCI
lessons.title: Food webs: pathways, roles and ripple effects
teach: A food-web arrow points from the energy/food source toward the organism receiving it. Read an arrow aloud as “provides food energy to.” A chain is one path; a web combines paths.

Producers build food using an energy source. Consumers obtain food from other organisms. Along a specified path, primary consumers eat producers; secondary consumers eat primary consumers; tertiary consumers eat secondary consumers. An omnivore may occupy different consumer levels on different paths.

Decomposers such as many fungi and bacteria break down remains and wastes, returning matter to the environment. Matter cycles; usable energy moves through the system and is eventually dispersed as heat. Decomposers act on material from every level, not only a final predator.

Removing a group can affect its food and its consumers, but real webs include alternatives. Explain a likely direction and a condition rather than saying every connected species must disappear. The packet’s “marine” example includes freshwater organisms; use the actual water environment rather than trusting that label.

model.prompt: Original web: algae→snail→fish→heron; algae→insect larva→fish. A change sharply reduces snails.
model.reasoning: Follow arrows: algae supplies food energy to snails, then fish receive it from snails. Find an alternative path: fish also eat insect larvae. Predict conditionally: fish lose one food source; effects depend partly on larva availability. Trace another possibility: less snail grazing could allow more algae, if other limits do not dominate. Keep matter cycling separate from energy flow.
model.answer: Fish lose the snail pathway but may use insect larvae. Effects depend on alternative food and other limits. Reduced grazing could affect algae, so trace more than one conditional pathway.

lessons.subject: SS
lessons.title: Religious beliefs and daily life
teach: Polytheism means belief in many gods. The assigned reading shows Egyptian gods and goddesses including Amun, Anubis, Horus, Ra, Thoth, Osiris, Isis, Seth, Sekhmet, Ptah, Hathor and Nephthys.
Egyptians connected gods with nature, royal authority and life after death. People offered prayers and gifts and built temples. Priests carried out religious rituals.
When explaining a belief, say Egyptians believed. A belief that pleasing gods helped the Nile flood is evidence about religion; it is not a scientific explanation of river flooding.
Afterlife means life after death. Ancient Egyptians held beliefs about a person’s continued existence after death. These beliefs influenced burial customs.

Objects such as food containers, furniture and jewelry could be placed in tombs because people believed they might be useful after death. The source also connects good conduct and religious practices with hopes for an afterlife.
A belief can explain why people made an object or followed a custom. It does not prove that every family could afford the same burial.

lessons.subject: SS
lessons.title: Mummies, tombs and preserving the body
teach: A mummy is a preserved body. Mummification is the process used to preserve a body. Embalming means treating a body to slow decay.

In the process described in the reading, embalmers cleaned the body, treated organs, used natron to dry it and wrapped it in linen. Canopic jars held certain organs. Details changed over Egypt’s long history.
Keep object and process separate: mummy = the preserved body; mummification = preparing and preserving it. Afterlife beliefs explain why this work mattered.
Canopic jars held certain organs removed during mummification. A sarcophagus is a large outer coffin, often stone. Neither word means the entire tomb.
A pyramid is a monumental building used as a royal tomb in ancient Egypt. Its purpose connects architecture, royal power and afterlife beliefs. Not every Egyptian was buried in a pyramid.

Giza and the Valley of the Kings are different burial places. Khufu’s Great Pyramid is at Giza; Tutankhamun’s tomb is in the Valley of the Kings. Do not use these place names as if they were one site.

lessons.subject: SS
lessons.title: Pharaoh and government officials
teach: The pharaoh was Egypt’s ruler. Egyptians regarded the pharaoh as divine, or connected with godly authority. The pharaoh made laws, defended Egypt and collected taxes, including wheat.
The pharaoh relied on officials. The vizier was a trusted chief adviser and chief judge. The chief treasurer collected taxes. The general of armies directed the military.

A bureaucracy is a system of government offices and officials. Different officials carried out different jobs for the pharaoh. Match an official to the job, rather than assuming the pharaoh did every task alone.

lessons.subject: SS
lessons.title: Old, Middle and New Kingdoms
teach: The Old Kingdom is strongly associated with large royal pyramids. Khufu is the pharaoh associated with the Great Pyramid at Giza.
Large building projects required planning, supplies and many workers with different skills. A monument is evidence of organized work as well as royal power.

Do not mix up the builders: Khufu is associated with the Great Pyramid; Imhotep is associated with Djoser’s earlier Step Pyramid. The textbook’s construction numbers and some names are unreliable, so use the well-supported ruler-and-monument link.
After the Old Kingdom, Egypt experienced periods of divided power. Mentuhotep II reunited Egypt. Historians connect this reunification with the beginning of the Middle Kingdom.
Reunite means bring together again. Menes and Mentuhotep II are not interchangeable: the classroom account links Menes with early unification and Mentuhotep II with a later reunification.
Learn the order rather than the textbook’s conflicting date ranges: Old Kingdom → divided rule → Mentuhotep II and the Middle Kingdom.
The Hyksos were rulers with origins in western Asia who controlled northern Egypt for part of the Second Intermediate Period. They were not one of Egypt’s three kingdom names.
Ahmose I led the defeat of Hyksos rule and helped reunify Egypt. He is connected with the start of the New Kingdom.

Remember the change: Hyksos rule in the north → Ahmose defeats their rule → New Kingdom. The textbook’s claim about iron weapons is misleading; the important tested connection is the change in rulers, not that claim.

lessons.subject: SS
lessons.title: Nile landforms and travel

sources.title: Assigned OER Ancient Egypt
sources.status: Named pages content-read; full course audit incomplete

teach: A delta is land deposited by a river near its mouth. The Nile Delta lies in northern Egypt, where the river reaches the Mediterranean Sea.
As the river slows, it can leave sediment and split into channels. The delta’s fertile land supported farming. A delta is not the same as rocky rapids upstream.
Cataracts are rocky rapids or rough stretches of a river. They can make travel by boat difficult. In this unit they are a geography term, not a medical term.
A route affected by cataracts may require travelers to change how they move goods. The Nile connected regions, but not every stretch was equally easy to navigate.

lessons.subject: SS
lessons.title: New Kingdom rulers and their evidence
teach: Hatshepsut was a female pharaoh of the New Kingdom. Her reign included trade expeditions and major building projects, including her temple at Deir el-Bahri.
She first served as regent for the young ThutmoseIII, her stepson and nephew, and later ruled as pharaoh. A regent governs for someone who cannot yet rule personally.
Hatshepsut was not the first woman ever to rule. Her monuments and inscriptions provide evidence of how she presented her achievements and authority.
Tutankhamun, often called King Tut, was a New Kingdom pharaoh who became ruler while young. He lived after Hatshepsut and before Ramses II.
His tomb in the Valley of the Kings was discovered in 1922 with many objects still inside. Those objects help researchers study royal burial, craftsmanship and beliefs about the afterlife.
Tomb objects are evidence of this royal burial. They do not prove every Egyptian owned the same goods or received the same burial.
Ramses II is also called Ramses the Great. He was a New Kingdom pharaoh associated with military campaigns, a peace treaty with the Hittites and many monuments.
The great temple at Abu Simbel is associated with Ramses II. Its large royal statues express the ruler’s power and importance.
A ruler can use both fighting and diplomacy. A peace treaty is an agreement between sides; it does not mean they were never in conflict.

lessons.subject: SS
lessons.title: Nile flooding and farming
teach: Nile floodwater left behind silt, or fine soil. This helped make the land beside the river fertile. The fertile river land is called Black Land; the nearby desert is called Red Land.
Farmers used irrigation: ditches, channels and basins moved or held water for crops. Wheat and barley supplied grain. Flax supplied fiber for linen.
Follow the process: floodwater leaves silt; fertile soil supports crops; irrigation directs water. Black Land and Red Land describe fertile river land and desert, not the two political regions.

lessons.subject: SS
lessons.title: Jobs and contributions
teach: An occupation is a job. A contribution is what that work provides for society. Name the job, describe what the person does, and connect the work to what others need.
Scribes read, wrote and kept records, including taxes, court cases and a census, which is a population count. Artisans made goods such as pottery, furniture and jewelry.

Farmers grew food and useful crops and raised animals. Food surplus means extra food beyond what is needed. A surplus helped some people specialize in other jobs. People depended on one another’s work.

lessons.subject: SS
lessons.title: Priests, soldiers and legal rights
teach: Priests performed religious ceremonies and rituals. The readings explain that Egyptians believed these rituals helped keep the gods pleased. Report this as an Egyptian belief, not as a scientific cause of flooding.

Soldiers defended Egypt. The OER reading says successful soldiers could receive land from the pharaoh and keep wealth from conquered lands. This could improve their social position; a reward was not guaranteed to every soldier.

The teacher’s society mystery states that women could own property and conduct business and had many of the same legal rights as men. This does not mean every woman and man had the same power or experience.

lessons.subject: SS
lessons.title: Reading the social pyramid
teach: A social class is a group with a similar position in society. A social pyramid shows rank: a small group at the top had more power; larger groups lower down had less power.
Read your teacher’s five diagram labels from top to bottom: Pharaoh; Priests and nobles; Traders, artisans, shopkeepers, and scribes; Farmers and herders; Unskilled workers.

The diagram’s bottom label is Unskilled workers. The readings also discuss enslaved people and servants below farmers. Do not replace the diagram’s exact label when the question asks for that diagram. Lower rank does not mean work was unimportant.

lessons.subject: SS
lessons.title: Upper and Lower Egypt
teach: The Nile flows north into the Mediterranean Sea. Upper Egypt is in the south, upstream. Lower Egypt is in the north, downstream, near the Nile Delta.
Upper and Lower describe positions along the river. They do not mean top and bottom on a page. Follow the river toward its mouth to move downstream.
Remember the pair: Upper Egypt = south and upstream; Lower Egypt = north and downstream, near the delta.

lessons.subject: SS
lessons.title: Two lands become one kingdom
teach: The assigned reading credits Menes with uniting Upper and Lower Egypt around3100 BCE. Uniting means bringing the two regions under one ruler. Memphis became an early capital, or center of government.
The red crown stood for Lower Egypt; the white crown stood for Upper Egypt. The double crown joined those symbols. It is evidence of a claim to rule both regions.

Historians connect unification with Narmer, but the exact link between the names Narmer and Menes is debated. For a question asking what your assigned text says, use Menes. Do not treat a debated identity as certain.
A dynasty is a line of rulers from the same family. Dynasty tells you how rule passes through a family; it does not name one building or one job.
A pharaoh was Egypt’s ruler. The government collected resources, organized projects and defended the country. A united kingdom still needed people to carry out that work.
Keep three ideas separate: a ruler is one person; a dynasty is a family line of rulers; a kingdom is the territory and people under a ruler.

lessons.subject: SS
lessons.title: Writing, artifacts and exchange
teach: Hieroglyphics is the classroom term for Egyptian writing using hieroglyphs. Signs could represent sounds or words; it was not simply an English letter-for-picture code.
Papyrus is a Nile plant and the paper-like writing material made from its stems. Scribes used writing skills to record information. Writing is a system of signs; papyrus is a material.

The Rosetta Stone contains three scripts: hieroglyphic, demotic and Greek, using two languages. The assigned text simplifies this incorrectly. Comparing the same message helped scholars decipher the writing.
An artifact is an object made or changed by people. Artifacts can provide evidence about tools, skills, beliefs or daily life, depending on their context.
A sphinx combines a human head and a lion’s body. The Great Sphinx stands at Giza, near the pyramid complex of Khafre. It is not in the Valley of the Kings, despite the textbook’s incorrect location.
An artifact’s shape or location supports some claims but not every claim. A royal monument can express power without representing how every Egyptian lived.
Commerce means buying, selling or exchanging goods. Egypt and Nubia traded resources, including grain and gold. Interdependence means groups depend on one another.

Cultural diffusion is the spread of ideas, knowledge, customs or styles between groups. It can occur through contact and trade, and also through migration or conquest; it is not limited to peaceful exchange.
Nubia had its own societies, rulers and traditions. Similarities with Egypt do not make the two societies identical. Nubian rulers later ruled Egypt, and Meroe became an important Nubian center.
